directions: Orange Princess is a hybrid globeflower selection valued for its warm tangerine-orange, buttercup-like blooms that open in late spring above mounds of deeply cut, glossy dark green foliage. Like other Trollius x cultorum hybrids, it demands consistently moist, humus-rich soil and resents drying out even briefly, making it a natural choice for a pond margin, streamside bed, or boggy border in cool partial shade. Deadhead spent flowers to tidy the clump, and divide congested crowns every three to four years in early autumn to keep flowering strong. In regions with hot summers, afternoon shade helps prevent the foliage from scorching and prolongs the bloom display.

American globeflower is a spring-blooming native of calcareous fens, wet meadows, and streamside seeps from the northeastern United States into the upper Midwest, bearing pale creamy-yellow to greenish-yellow, half-open globes held just above clumps of finely divided leaves. It is shorter and earlier-flowering than the European and Asian globeflowers grown in gardens, and it is an excellent choice for a native wetland planting, rain garden, or bog bed where the soil never dries out. Because wild populations have declined in parts of its range from wetland drainage, nursery-propagated plants or responsibly sourced divisions are the appropriate choice for garden stock. Give it constant moisture, cool roots, and light shade in warmer zones to keep it thriving for years.

Giant marsh marigold is a robust, sprawling relative of the familiar marsh marigold, producing much larger glossy, heart-shaped leaves and bigger golden-yellow, buttercup-like flowers carried on thick hollow stems that root as they creep along the mud. It spreads readily by these creeping stolons across the margins of ponds, streams, and bog gardens, quickly forming an expansive colony where it has room to roam, so it suits larger water features better than small garden pools. Plant it in saturated soil or shallow water at the pond edge in partial shade to full sun, where it will flower over an extended period from mid-spring into summer. Because of its vigorous spreading habit, site it where its expansion is welcome or contain the roots with a buried barrier.

Chilean rhubarb is a bold architectural perennial related to the more commonly grown Gunnera manicata, producing large, coarsely toothed, rounded leaves on thick, bristly stalks that form a dramatic clump at the edge of a pond, stream, or bog garden. It is generally considered somewhat more compact and cold-tolerant than G. manicata, though it still needs deep, constantly moist, rich soil and shelter from drying wind to develop its full size. In summer it sends up unusual cone-shaped reddish-brown flower spikes from the base of the plant, followed by small orange seed clusters that add further interest. In cold winters, mulch the dormant crown heavily with straw or its own cut foliage to protect it from hard freezes.

Often called dwarf gunnera, this low, mat-forming groundcover is a diminutive relative of the giant ornamental rhubarbs, spreading by creeping rhizomes to form a dense carpet of small, rounded, lobed leaves only a few inches tall. It thrives in consistently damp, humus-rich soil at the edge of a bog garden, stream, or shaded rock garden, where its cool green mat contrasts nicely with larger-leaved moisture lovers nearby. Tiny reddish flower spikes appear at ground level in summer, followed by small orange-red fruits. Unlike its giant cousins it needs no elaborate winter protection beyond a reliably moist, sheltered site, though a light mulch helps in the colder part of its range.
sources: Great Plant Picks (Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden)

directions: Winter heliotrope is grown chiefly for its wonderfully fragrant, vanilla-almond-scented flower clusters that appear on short stalks in the depths of winter, often before the rounded, glossy leaves have fully unfurled. It spreads aggressively by rhizomes to form a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover in damp shade, along woodland edges, or at a pond margin, and this vigor means it is best confined to naturalized areas or contained beds rather than mixed perennial borders. Once established it is extremely tough and long-lived, tolerating deep shade, heavy soil, and periodic flooding with equanimity. Because of its spreading habit, site it away from smaller, less competitive plants and consider a buried root barrier where space is limited.

Ornamental Chinese rhubarb is a dramatic architectural perennial grown for its enormous, deeply cut, palmately lobed leaves that can span several feet across, unfurling from thick crowns in early spring atop stout, often reddish leaf stalks. In early summer it sends up towering, plume-like flower spikes in shades of creamy white to deep pink well above the foliage, adding a second season of interest before the seed heads turn tan and papery. It performs best in deep, rich, constantly moist soil at a streamside or pond margin, with a little afternoon shade helping to prevent leaf scorch in hot climates. Give it plenty of room, since a mature clump can rival a large shrub in both height and spread.

Atrosanguineum is a striking dark-leaved selection of ornamental Chinese rhubarb, emerging in spring with deeply lobed leaves flushed an intense blackish-red that gradually fades toward green as the season progresses, though the undersides and veins often retain a rich red cast. Tall plumes of crimson-red flowers rise well above the foliage in early summer, echoing the leaf color and making this one of the most dramatic accents available for a damp border or bog garden. Like the species, it needs deep, humus-rich, constantly moist soil and benefits from a little afternoon shade in hot regions to keep the foliage from scorching and to prolong its rich coloring. Divide congested crowns in early spring or fall if the clump outgrows its space or flowering declines.
